options.text: A traffic spike that exceeded the site's capacity
options.rationale: Accurate as a description of the symptom, but it doesn't classify the outage.

questions.explanation: A friendly or unintentional DoS is an outage with no malicious intent, such as viral demand, a misconfiguration, or a runaway process. The surge is the symptom; intent is what separates it from a DDoS.
questions.discriminator_tested: No attacker: intent is what separates a friendly DoS from a DDoS.

questions.stem: Which two events would take services offline without generating any malicious network traffic? (Choose two.)

options.text: An intruder cuts the fiber cable outside the building
options.rationale: Correct: a physical attack on infrastructure.

options.text: Spoofed ICMP replies overload the core router CPU
options.rationale: That is malicious ICMP traffic.

options.text: Someone turns off the server room's power
options.rationale: Correct: powering off infrastructure is a physical attack.

options.text: A worm spreads between servers and crashes services
options.rationale: A worm moves over the network.

options.text: A botnet floods the web server with HTTP requests
options.rationale: A DDoS is carried by malicious traffic.

questions.explanation: A physical attack damages, cuts, or powers off infrastructure. It hits availability with no network traffic at all, so network monitoring may show nothing but silence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Physical attacks hit availability with no network traffic.

questions.stem: After an attack, three branch routers no longer boot. Power-cycling them and reloading the saved configuration both fail, and the vendor says the boot code itself is damaged and must be reflashed. Which attack fits?

options.text: A SYN flood exhausting the connection state
options.rationale: A flood ends when the traffic stops; a reboot would clear it.

options.text: A friendly DoS from a configuration mistake
options.rationale: There was an attack, and configuration errors don't damage boot code.

options.text: A permanent DoS against the devices' firmware
options.rationale: Correct: corrupted firmware needs a reflash or replacement.

options.text: Ransomware encrypting the saved configuration
options.rationale: The configuration reloaded but the boot code is what failed.

questions.explanation: A permanent DoS corrupts device firmware so the device is unusable. A reboot won't fix it; it needs a reflash or replacement, unlike floods, which end when the traffic stops.
questions.discriminator_tested: Permanent DoS needs reflash or replacement; a reboot won't fix it.

questions.stem: A capture on a partner's network segment shows the traffic below. The host at 203.0.113.50 says it never sent any pings and is being overwhelmed. Which attack name BEST fits?
questions.exhibit:
No.  Source           Destination       Protocol  Info
1    203.0.113.50     198.51.100.255    ICMP      Echo (ping) request
2    198.51.100.12    203.0.113.50      ICMP      Echo (ping) reply
3    198.51.100.13    203.0.113.50      ICMP      Echo (ping) reply
4    198.51.100.14    203.0.113.50      ICMP      Echo (ping) reply
5    198.51.100.15    203.0.113.50      ICMP      Echo (ping) reply
...  (hundreds more replies per second)

options.text: Smurf attack
options.rationale: Correct: echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source, so every host replies to the victim.

options.text: SYN flood
options.rationale: A SYN flood uses TCP handshakes, not ICMP echo.

options.text: Reflection attack
options.rationale: Technically true, since the segment's hosts bounce the traffic, but the broadcast echo pattern has a more specific name.

options.text: ARP spoofing
options.rationale: ARP spoofing forges MAC-to-IP mappings; it doesn't flood with ICMP.

questions.explanation: A smurf attack sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source IP, so every host on that segment replies to the victim. It is a kind of reflection attack, but the broadcast echo pattern is what names it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smurf: ICMP echo to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source.

questions.stem: Users can't open new connections to a web server, although sessions that were already open keep working. The admin runs netstat. Which explanation BEST fits the output?
questions.exhibit:
Proto  Local Address    Foreign Address       State
TCP    10.0.0.5:443     198.18.44.10:51022    SYN_RECEIVED
TCP    10.0.0.5:443     198.18.97.3:40211     SYN_RECEIVED
TCP    10.0.0.5:443     198.19.2.77:61873     SYN_RECEIVED
TCP    10.0.0.5:443     198.18.150.9:33090    SYN_RECEIVED
... 4,812 more in SYN_RECEIVED; 37 ESTABLISHED

options.text: A flood of ICMP echo replies is saturating the link
options.rationale: The output shows TCP state, not ICMP; a saturated link would hurt existing sessions too.

options.text: The site's TLS certificate has expired for new visitors
options.rationale: An expired certificate produces browser warnings, not half-open TCP entries.

options.text: A denial of service is exhausting the server's resources
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't identify the mechanism the output shows.

options.text: Half-open handshakes are filling the connection table
options.rationale: Correct: thousands of SYN_RECEIVED entries that never complete leave no room for new clients.

questions.explanation: A SYN flood sends TCP SYNs and never completes the handshake, so half-open (SYN_RECEIVED) entries fill the connection table and new clients are refused. 'Denial of service' is true but doesn't identify the mechanism.
questions.discriminator_tested: SYN flood fills the half-open connection table.

questions.stem: Attackers send 60-byte DNS queries carrying the victim's spoofed address to thousands of open resolvers, and each resolver sends a 3,000-byte answer to the victim. Which statement BEST explains why this technique is so effective?

options.text: The victim's half-open connection table fills with DNS sessions
options.rationale: DNS answers over UDP don't create half-open TCP entries.

options.text: The resolvers' caches are poisoned and send users to the wrong IP
options.rationale: Cache poisoning misdirects users; nothing here alters resolver records.

options.text: The attackers hide their own addresses behind spoofed source IPs
options.rationale: True, but hiding the source doesn't explain the overwhelming volume.

options.text: Third parties reflect it, and each reply dwarfs its request
options.rationale: Correct: reflection plus amplification, here about 50 times.

questions.explanation: In reflective and amplified attacks, spoofed requests go to third-party servers that send their responses to the victim (reflective), and each response is much larger than the request (amplified).
questions.discriminator_tested: Reflective = a third party bounces it; amplified = response larger than request.

questions.stem: On hotel Wi-Fi, a traveler's banking session suddenly shows a certificate warning, which the traveler clicks through. Later the bank reports that a transfer amount was changed in transit. What BEST explains both events?

options.text: A keylogger on the laptop captured the traveler's banking password
options.rationale: Stolen keystrokes explain neither the certificate warning nor the altered transfer.

options.text: The bank's server was overloaded and corrupted the transfer data
options.rationale: Overload causes failures, not certificate warnings or targeted changes.

options.text: Someone between the traveler and the bank altered traffic
options.rationale: Correct: an on-path attacker presented its own certificate and changed the live session.

options.text: Someone read the traveler's traffic on the shared wireless network
options.rationale: Eavesdropping breaks confidentiality but can't change the transfer amount.

questions.explanation: An on-path attack (formerly called man-in-the-middle, MitM) places the attacker between two parties to read or alter a live session. The altered transfer shows integrity was broken, not only confidentiality.
questions.discriminator_tested: On-path breaks confidentiality and integrity of a live session.

questions.stem: Several users type the correct address of the company intranet, but their browsers land on a look-alike login page hosted at an unfamiliar IP address. Users who connect by IP address instead of by name are fine. Which attack BEST fits?

options.text: Phishing email
options.rationale: The users typed the correct address themselves; no fraudulent link was involved.

options.text: DNS cache poisoning
options.rationale: Correct: the right name resolves to the wrong IP; connecting by IP bypasses the bad record.

options.text: Evil twin access point
options.rationale: Users on wired and wireless links alike reached the wrong IP by name only.

options.text: ARP spoofing
options.rationale: ARP spoofing would affect traffic by IP as well, and only on the local subnet.

questions.explanation: DNS poisoning inserts false records into a resolver or cache: the user enters the right name and reaches the wrong IP. Connecting by IP address bypasses DNS, which is why those users were unaffected.
questions.discriminator_tested: User enters the right name, reaches the wrong IP.

questions.stem: An IDS flags the frame below arriving on a user's switch port. What is the sender MOST likely attempting?
questions.exhibit:
Ethernet II   src 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e
  802.1Q tag  VLAN 1    (outer)
  802.1Q tag  VLAN 30   (inner)
  IPv4        10.30.0.15 -> 10.30.0.20
Ingress port: Gi0/7 (access port, VLAN 1)
Uplink trunk native VLAN: 1

options.text: Becoming a trunk by negotiating with the switch as a switch
options.rationale: Switch spoofing is the other VLAN-hopping method, but this frame shows stacked tags, not trunk negotiation.

options.text: Mapping its MAC to another host's IP with forged replies
options.rationale: That is ARP spoofing; nothing in the frame is an ARP reply.

options.text: Flooding the switch's MAC table so frames go out each port
options.rationale: MAC flooding sends many source addresses, not one double-tagged frame.

options.text: Reaching VLAN 30 by double tagging through the native VLAN
options.rationale: Correct: the switch strips the outer native-VLAN tag and forwards the frame carrying the inner VLAN 30 tag.

questions.explanation: VLAN hopping reaches a VLAN you aren't assigned to, by switch spoofing or double tagging. Double tagging exploits the native VLAN: the first switch removes the outer tag matching the native VLAN and forwards the frame with the inner tag.
questions.discriminator_tested: Double tagging exploits the native VLAN.

questions.stem: The security team says another host is reading a user's traffic. On the user's PC, 10.20.1.1 is the default gateway and 10.20.1.37 is a colleague's laptop. Given the output, what is the MOST likely explanation?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> arp -a
Interface: 10.20.1.44
  Internet Address    Physical Address     Type
  10.20.1.1           8c-16-45-aa-01-02    dynamic
  10.20.1.37          8c-16-45-aa-01-02    dynamic
  10.20.1.50          3c-52-82-11-9e-40    dynamic

options.text: False DNS records point the gateway's name at the laptop
options.rationale: The table maps IPs to MACs; DNS plays no part in it.

options.text: Forged replies tied the gateway's IP to the laptop's MAC
options.rationale: Correct: two IPs share one MAC because the laptop answered for the gateway.

options.text: Traffic for the gateway is being relayed through the laptop
options.rationale: That is the result (an on-path position), not the mechanism the output reveals.

options.text: The gateway and laptop share one network card by design
options.rationale: Two different hosts can't legitimately share a physical address.

questions.explanation: ARP spoofing sends forged ARP replies so the attacker's MAC maps to another host's IP, here the gateway. It works only on the local subnet and commonly enables an on-path attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: ARP spoofing is local-subnet only and commonly enables on-path.

questions.stem: New laptops on the third floor receive addresses with a default gateway of 10.9.9.9, which isn't the company router, and their web traffic is being captured. Older machines that kept their existing leases are fine. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The laptops are sending traffic to an attacker's gateway
options.rationale: That is the consequence, not the cause of the bad settings.

options.text: An unauthorized server handing out settings on that floor
options.rationale: Correct: a rogue DHCP server answers new lease requests with its own gateway.

options.text: The router's DHCP pool ran out of addresses for new devices
options.rationale: An empty pool gives no address at all, not a different gateway.

options.text: A forged ARP reply is redirecting the router's IP address
options.rationale: ARP spoofing wouldn't change the gateway address the laptops were given.

questions.explanation: A rogue DHCP server is an unauthorized DHCP server that hands out a bad gateway or DNS server. Only clients requesting new leases are affected. DHCP snooping counters it by accepting offers only from trusted ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rogue DHCP hands out a bad gateway/DNS; countered by DHCP snooping.

questions.stem: A company plans to add 200 smart cameras to its network. Which two weaknesses MOST often turn devices like these into botnet recruits? (Choose two.)

options.text: Cameras placed on their own isolated VLAN
options.rationale: Isolation is a mitigation, not a weakness.

options.text: Power drawn over Ethernet instead of mains
options.rationale: PoE has no bearing on compromise.

options.text: Vendor default logins left unchanged after install
options.rationale: Correct: malware simply logs in with the factory credentials.

options.text: Video streams sent without any encryption
options.rationale: A real IoT weakness, but it exposes the video rather than handing over control of the device.

options.text: Firmware that goes unpatched for years
options.rationale: Correct: known flaws stay exploitable at scale.

questions.explanation: IoT vulnerabilities include default credentials, unpatched firmware, and weak or no encryption. Default logins and unpatched firmware let malware take over devices at scale, which makes IoT a frequent source of botnet recruits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Default credentials and unpatched firmware make IoT botnet recruits.

questions.stem: A wireless scan finds an access point broadcasting 'Lab-Test' that is cabled into a conference-room wall jack. No one in IT installed it, and it has no password. Which threat does this device BEST represent?

options.text: A rogue AP: an unauthorized backdoor into the wired LAN
options.rationale: Correct: it sits inside the network and bypasses the perimeter.

options.text: An open hotspot that lets nearby users browse the web
options.rationale: True of the device, but it misses the real risk: access to the internal network.

options.text: An evil twin: a fake copy of the company's own network
options.rationale: An evil twin imitates a legitimate SSID to lure users; 'Lab-Test' imitates nothing.

options.text: A permanent DoS: a device that disrupts the wireless band
options.rationale: Nothing suggests interference or bricked devices.

questions.explanation: A rogue AP is an unauthorized access point plugged into the wired network. It sits inside your network as a backdoor; an evil twin imitates a legitimate SSID and targets users instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rogue AP sits inside the network; evil twin targets users.

questions.stem: At an airport, staff laptops list two networks named 'CorpGuest'. The stronger one isn't the company's, and anyone who joins it sees a sign-in page asking for corporate credentials. What is this?

options.text: A DNS poisoning attack on the guest resolver
options.rationale: The fake page comes from joining the wrong network, not from bad DNS records.

options.text: A rogue AP connected to the company's own LAN
options.rationale: A rogue AP is plugged into your network; this one is the attacker's, at an airport.

options.text: An evil twin posing as the real guest network
options.rationale: Correct: an attacker AP imitating a legitimate SSID to capture credentials.

options.text: A smishing message sent to travelling staff
options.rationale: No text message is involved.

questions.explanation: An evil twin is an attacker AP imitating a legitimate SSID. It targets users, often to capture credentials; a rogue AP is an unauthorized device inside your own network.
questions.discriminator_tested: Evil twin imitates an SSID to target users.

questions.stem: Files on a shared drive suddenly have a new extension and can't be opened, and a text file in each folder demands cryptocurrency for a key. Which response is the BEST first step?

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on the file server
options.rationale: Useful later; scanning while connected doesn't stop the spread.

options.text: Pay the demand so the business can resume quickly
options.rationale: Paying doesn't stop the spread or guarantee a working key.

options.text: Restore the encrypted files from the latest backup
options.rationale: Needed, but restoring first lets the still-running malware encrypt the restored files.

options.text: Disconnect the affected systems from the network
options.rationale: Correct: containment stops the encryption spreading.

questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment for the key: extortion for access. Containing it first stops the encryption from spreading; restoring from backup comes after the ransomware is removed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ransomware holds data for payment; contain before restoring.

questions.stem: An employee installs a free PDF converter from a download site. It converts files as promised, but it also opens a hidden remote-access connection. It has not spread to any other machine. Which malware type BEST fits?

options.text: Virus
options.rationale: A virus attaches to existing files; this was a standalone program the user installed.

options.text: Adware
options.rationale: Adware pushes ads; this opened remote access.

options.text: Trojan
options.rationale: Correct: disguised as useful software, run by the user, and not self-replicating.

options.text: Worm
options.rationale: A worm spreads by itself; this stayed on one machine.

questions.explanation: A Trojan is malicious code disguised as legitimate software. The user must run it, and it doesn't self-replicate, which is why it stayed on one machine.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trojan: user runs it; it does not self-replicate.

questions.stem: Within an hour of one unpatched server being infected, 400 other servers on the same network are infected. No one opened a file or clicked anything, and no existing programs were modified. Which malware type is this?

options.text: Virus
options.rationale: A virus needs a host file and user action to spread.

options.text: Worm
options.rationale: Correct: self-replicating over the network, no user action, no host file.

options.text: Rootkit
options.rationale: A rootkit hides access; it isn't a spreading mechanism.

options.text: Trojan
options.rationale: A Trojan doesn't self-replicate.

questions.explanation: A worm is self-replicating malware that spreads over networks with no user action and no host file. A virus needs a host and user action to spread.
questions.discriminator_tested: Worm spreads with no user action and no host file.

questions.stem: Malware is found inside several spreadsheets on a shared drive. Which two characteristics would confirm it is a virus rather than a worm? (Choose two.)

options.text: It posed as a useful program so the user would install it
options.rationale: That describes a Trojan.

options.text: It copies itself across the network with no one involved
options.rationale: That describes a worm.

options.text: It is attached to legitimate files rather than standing alone
options.rationale: Correct: a virus needs a host file.

options.text: It hides in the kernel to conceal itself and other malware
options.rationale: That describes a rootkit.

options.text: It needs someone to open an infected file
options.rationale: Correct: a virus needs user action.

questions.explanation: A virus is malicious code that attaches to a legitimate file or program; it needs a host and user action to spread. A worm self-replicates over the network without either.
questions.discriminator_tested: Virus needs a host file and user action to spread.

questions.stem: A user's laptop shows no pop-ups or slowdowns, but the security team finds software silently sending browsing history, screenshots, and the contact list to an outside server every night. Which category BEST describes it?

options.text: Spyware
options.rationale: Correct: covert collection of activity and data.

options.text: Adware
options.rationale: Adware delivers ads; there are none here.

options.text: Ransomware
options.rationale: Nothing is encrypted or held for payment.

options.text: Keylogger
options.rationale: A keylogger captures keystrokes, one narrow method; this gathers far more.

questions.explanation: Spyware secretly collects user activity and data; its goal is covert information gathering. Adware focuses on ads, and a keylogger is one specific capture method that spyware may use.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spyware's goal is covert information gathering.

questions.stem: A small USB adapter is found between a keyboard and the reception PC. The receptionist's email and VPN passwords were later used from abroad, but a full scan finds no suspicious software on the PC. Which threat BEST explains the stolen passwords?

options.text: A Trojan installed from a fake download
options.rationale: A Trojan is software; the scan found nothing installed.

options.text: Spyware quietly collecting user activity
options.rationale: Spyware is software, and the scan found none.

options.text: A hardware keylogger capturing keystrokes
options.rationale: Correct: an inline device records every key typed, invisible to software scans.

options.text: Shoulder surfing at the reception desk
options.rationale: Possible in principle, but it ignores the device found on the keyboard cable.

questions.explanation: A keylogger records keystrokes to capture credentials and other input. It is a specific capture method, often delivered by spyware or a Trojan, and it can also be a small hardware device that no software scan sees.
questions.discriminator_tested: Keylogger = a specific keystroke-capture method.

questions.stem: Antivirus on a server reports nothing, yet network monitoring shows the server talking to an unknown host. A scan from a clean boot USB finds modified kernel drivers that hide certain processes and files from the running operating system. What BEST describes this malware?

options.text: Spyware sending data to an outside host
options.rationale: The traffic might carry data, but the kernel-level hiding is the key finding.

options.text: A worm spreading through the server's drivers
options.rationale: Nothing shows self-replication to other systems.

options.text: Malware with privileged access to the server
options.rationale: True, but privilege alone doesn't capture its defining trait: hiding.

options.text: A rootkit concealing itself and other malware
options.rationale: Correct: defined by kernel-level concealment.

questions.explanation: A rootkit hides deep in the OS, kernel, or firmware to keep privileged, stealthy access. It is defined by concealment: it hides itself and other malware, which is why a scan from a clean boot finds what the infected OS hides.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rootkit is defined by concealment.

questions.stem: After a user installs a free video player, the browser's home page changes, new toolbars appear, and pop-up offers show on most sites, slowing the PC down. Nothing is encrypted and no data theft is found. Which category fits BEST?

options.text: Ransomware
options.rationale: Nothing is encrypted or held for payment.

options.text: Malvertising
options.rationale: Malvertising rides on ad networks on legitimate sites; this came with installed software.

options.text: Adware
options.rationale: Correct: unwanted ads bundled with free software.

options.text: Spyware
options.rationale: No covert data collection was found; the symptoms are ads.

questions.explanation: Adware delivers unwanted ads, often bundled with free software. Its focus is nuisance and tracking and it may degrade performance; malvertising instead rides on ad networks serving legitimate sites.
questions.discriminator_tested: Adware = nuisance ads bundled with software.

questions.stem: Visitors to a reputable news site are redirected to an exploit page. The site's own servers and code are clean; the redirect comes from a banner served by a third-party ad network. Which term BEST describes this attack?

options.text: Drive-by download
options.rationale: The exploit page may deliver one, but the defining route here is the ad network.

options.text: DNS poisoning
options.rationale: The site name resolved correctly; the ad itself redirected users.

options.text: Adware
options.rationale: Adware is unwanted ad software on the user's own machine.

options.text: Malvertising
options.rationale: Correct: the attack rides on the ad network, not the site.

questions.explanation: Malvertising places malicious ads on legitimate sites to redirect visitors or deliver malware. The attack rides on ad networks; the site itself isn't compromised.
questions.discriminator_tested: Malvertising rides on ad networks; the site isn't compromised.

questions.stem: A honeypot that records attempted passwords logs the entries below. Which description BEST fits these attempts?
questions.exhibit:
10:02:11  user=admin  password=aaaa  result=fail
10:02:11  user=admin  password=aaab  result=fail
10:02:11  user=admin  password=aaac  result=fail
10:02:12  user=admin  password=aaad  result=fail
...       (11,880 attempts in 40 minutes, all from 198.51.100.7)

options.text: A denial of service against the SSH service
options.rationale: The goal is to find the password, not to exhaust the service.

options.text: A dictionary attack using a list of likely words
options.rationale: A dictionary attack tries likely passwords, not sequential strings.

options.text: Brute force, trying combinations in order
options.rationale: Correct: aaaa, aaab, aaac is an exhaustive sequence.

options.text: A password attack against the admin account
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say which kind of attack the pattern reveals.

questions.explanation: Brute force tries every possible combination: exhaustive and slow. The sequence aaaa, aaab, aaac is not a list of likely passwords as a dictionary attack uses. Lockouts and long passwords defeat it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Brute force is exhaustive; dictionary guesses likely passwords.

questions.stem: An attacker copies a password-hash file and runs a tool that hashes 'password1', 'Summer2024!', 'qwerty', and 14 million other entries from a leaked-password list, comparing each to the stolen hashes. Which statement BEST describes this attack?

options.text: It works through each possible character combination in turn
options.rationale: That is brute force; a list of 14 million leaked passwords is not exhaustive.

options.text: It replays captured sessions to skip the password check
options.rationale: Session replay doesn't involve guessing passwords at all.

options.text: It is an offline password attack against stolen hashes
options.rationale: True, but that doesn't separate it from an offline brute-force attack.

options.text: It tries likely passwords, not each combination
options.rationale: Correct: a dictionary attack works from a precompiled list.

questions.explanation: A dictionary attack tries words from a precompiled list: it guesses likely passwords, not all of them. Blocking common passwords counters it; brute force is the exhaustive version.
questions.discriminator_tested: Dictionary attack guesses likely passwords, not all of them.

questions.stem: Investigators find that intruders entered a defense contractor 14 months ago through a tailored email, then quietly moved between systems and copied engineering files in small amounts each week. Which term BEST describes this threat?

options.text: An advanced persistent threat
options.rationale: Correct: stealthy, targeted, and long-term.

options.text: A coordinated attack
options.rationale: Coordination between actors isn't the defining trait; persistence is.

options.text: A spear-phishing campaign
options.rationale: True of how they got in, but it describes only the entry, not the 14-month intrusion.

options.text: An insider threat
options.rationale: The intruders came from outside; no one with legitimate access caused it.

questions.explanation: An advanced persistent threat (APT) is a stealthy, long-term, targeted intrusion, often well-resourced. It is defined by persistence and dwell time; spear phishing was only the way in.
questions.discriminator_tested: APT is defined by persistence and dwell time.

questions.stem: A company requires that each network device's vendor login be replaced before the device is connected. Which threat does this control MOST directly address?

options.text: Unauthorized access to the network devices in general
options.rationale: True in a broad sense, but not the specific threat this control targets.

options.text: Attackers guessing weak passwords that staff chose
options.rationale: That risk is addressed by blocking common passwords.

options.text: Attackers logging in with published factory passwords
options.rationale: Correct: vendor logins are documented and widely known.

options.text: Attackers exploiting unpatched firmware on devices
options.rationale: Firmware flaws are fixed by upgrading firmware, not by changing logins.

questions.explanation: Changing default credentials replaces vendor logins before deployment. It counters default-login exploitation, the main way IoT botnets recruit devices; avoiding common passwords counters dictionary attacks instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Changing default credentials counters default-login exploitation.

questions.stem: A password audit shows many staff use passwords like 'Welcome1' and 'Spring2025!'. They meet the length and complexity rules. Which control BEST addresses the specific risk these passwords create?

options.text: Locking accounts after five failed sign-in attempts
options.rationale: Slows online guessing but does nothing about offline cracking of predictable passwords.

options.text: Forcing users to change their passwords each month
options.rationale: Frequent changes push people toward patterns like 'Spring2025!'.

options.text: Rejecting passwords that appear on known-breached lists
options.rationale: Correct: it stops exactly the passwords guess lists try first.

options.text: Raising the minimum password length to 16 characters
options.rationale: Helps against brute force, but 'Welcome1Welcome1' would still pass.

questions.explanation: Avoiding common passwords means blocking easily guessed passwords. It counters dictionary attacks, which try likely passwords first; 'Welcome1' meets complexity rules but sits near the top of guess lists.
questions.discriminator_tested: Blocking common passwords counters dictionary attacks.

questions.stem: Which switch configuration BEST prevents a device plugged into a user port from handing out IP settings to other clients?

options.text: Move the native VLAN off the default VLAN
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

options.text: Enable port security with one learned MAC
options.rationale: The rogue server can be that one MAC address.

options.text: Shut down unused switch ports across the building
options.rationale: Reduces exposure, but a device on any in-use port could still answer.

options.text: Trust DHCP offers only from the uplink
options.rationale: Correct: DHCP snooping ignores offers arriving on untrusted ports.

questions.explanation: DHCP snooping is a switch feature that accepts DHCP offers only from trusted ports. It counters rogue DHCP: user ports are untrusted, so a server plugged into one is ignored.
questions.discriminator_tested: DHCP snooping trusts offers only from trusted ports.

questions.stem: A switch audit finds that each trunk uses VLAN 1 as its native VLAN, and user access ports are also in VLAN 1. Which change BEST closes the double-tagging path between VLANs?

options.text: Turn off trunk negotiation on the user ports
options.rationale: That counters switch spoofing, the other VLAN-hopping method.

options.text: Move the user access ports into a different VLAN
options.rationale: Also breaks the precondition today, but the next port left in VLAN 1 reopens the path.

options.text: Set the trunks' native VLAN to an unused VLAN ID
options.rationale: Correct: an unused native VLAN means no user port can match it.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on the access switches
options.rationale: DHCP snooping counters rogue DHCP, not VLAN hopping.

questions.explanation: Changing the native VLAN moves it off the default. Double tagging only works when the attacker's access VLAN matches the trunk's native VLAN, so an unused native VLAN removes the path; disabling negotiation counters switch spoofing instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Changing the native VLAN counters double tagging.

questions.stem: A vendor releases a fix for a remotely exploitable flaw in the web server application that runs on the company's Linux servers. Which activity applies this fix?

options.text: Patching and updating the installed software
options.rationale: Correct: the flaw is in an application.

options.text: Changing the servers' default administrator logins
options.rationale: Good hardening, but it doesn't remove a code flaw.

options.text: Upgrading the firmware on the server hardware
options.rationale: Firmware is device-level code; the flaw is in application software.

options.text: Restarting the servers to clear the running code
options.rationale: A restart reloads the same flawed code.

questions.explanation: Patching and updating fixes known vulnerabilities in software such as an operating system or application. Upgrading firmware updates device-level code embedded in hardware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Patching = software; firmware = device-level code.

questions.stem: A vulnerability is found in the UEFI code that starts the company's laptops before the operating system loads. Windows Update offers no fix; the laptop maker publishes one. What kind of update is needed?

options.text: An application update
options.rationale: No application is involved.

options.text: A firmware upgrade
options.rationale: Correct: UEFI is code embedded in the hardware.

options.text: An operating system patch
options.rationale: The flaw runs before the OS loads, which is why Windows Update can't fix it.

options.text: A configuration reset
options.rationale: Resetting settings leaves the flawed code in place.

questions.explanation: Upgrading firmware updates device-level code embedded in hardware, such as UEFI, which runs before the OS. OS and application patching fix software instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Firmware is embedded in hardware; contrast with OS/app patching.

questions.stem: A phishing email gets past the email filter, but endpoint protection blocks the attachment. Had it run, the user's standard account and the network's segmentation would still have limited it. Which principle does this BEST illustrate?

options.text: Least privilege
options.rationale: One of the layers involved, but the scenario shows the layering itself.

options.text: Security through obscurity
options.rationale: Nothing relies on hiding how the system works.

options.text: Defense in depth
options.rationale: Correct: several overlapping layers, none relied on alone.

options.text: Separation of duties
options.rationale: Splitting tasks between people isn't shown here.

questions.explanation: Defense in depth uses layered, overlapping controls so that no single control is relied on. Each layer here caught or limited what the one before it missed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Defense in depth: no single control is relied on.

questions.stem: A security awareness course will cover social engineering. Which two incidents is it designed to help prevent? (Choose two.)

options.text: A fake courier talks his way into the server room
options.rationale: Correct: a person was manipulated in person.

options.text: A brute-force tool cracks a weak VPN password
options.rationale: A technical attack on a password, not on a person.

options.text: A worm exploits an unpatched SMB service overnight
options.rationale: A technical exploit; patching addresses it.

options.text: A failed disk takes the file server offline
options.rationale: A hardware fault, not an attack on people.

options.text: A caller posing as IT gets a user to read out a code
options.rationale: Correct: a person was manipulated by phone.

questions.explanation: Social engineering manipulates people rather than systems. It is the umbrella for phishing variants and physical-access tricks such as impersonation and piggybacking.
questions.discriminator_tested: Social engineering manipulates people rather than systems.

questions.stem: A database administrator accidentally runs a cleanup script against production instead of test and deletes six months of orders. There was no malicious intent. How is this incident BEST classified?

options.text: An accidental insider threat
options.rationale: Correct: harm from someone with legitimate access, without intent.

options.text: A friendly denial of service
options.rationale: Data was destroyed, not just made temporarily unavailable.

options.text: A configuration error
options.rationale: Describes the mistake, but not the threat category it belongs to.

options.text: A ransomware attack
options.rationale: Nothing was encrypted or held for payment.

questions.explanation: Insider threats are harm from someone with legitimate access, malicious or accidental. The administrator was already inside the perimeter; intent can be either.
questions.discriminator_tested: Insider threat intent can be malicious or accidental.

questions.stem: Thousands of a delivery company's customers receive the same email saying a parcel is held, with a link to pay a $1.99 redelivery fee on a look-alike site. The message uses no names or personal details. Which term BEST fits?

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: The medium is email, not SMS.

options.text: Whaling
options.rationale: Whaling targets executives.

options.text: Phishing
options.rationale: Correct: broad and untargeted.

options.text: Spear phishing
options.rationale: Spear phishing uses personal detail for a chosen target.

questions.explanation: Phishing uses fraudulent messages, typically email, to steal data or credentials. It is broad and untargeted; spear phishing uses personal detail for a chosen target.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phishing is broad and untargeted.

questions.stem: An employee gets a call from someone claiming to be the bank's fraud team. The caller reads out the last four digits of the company card and asks the employee to confirm the full number and security code. Which term BEST describes this?

options.text: Whaling
options.rationale: Whaling targets executives; nothing says this employee is one.

options.text: Phishing
options.rationale: Technically it is a form of phishing, but the voice medium has a more precise name.

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: Smishing uses text messages.

options.text: Vishing
options.rationale: Correct: phishing carried out by voice.

questions.explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice or phone: the medium is voice. It is a form of phishing, but the medium is what names it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Vishing: medium = voice.

questions.stem: Several staff receive the message below on their company phones. Which term BEST describes it?
questions.exhibit:
From: +1 (555) 014-2287
USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address.
Update within 24h: https://usps-redeliver.example.top/track

options.text: Phishing
options.rationale: Technically true, but the SMS medium has a more precise name.

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: Correct: phishing delivered by text message.

options.text: Spear phishing
options.rationale: The message has no personal detail; it is untargeted.

options.text: Vishing
options.rationale: Vishing uses voice calls.

questions.explanation: Smishing is phishing by SMS or text message: the medium is the text. It is a kind of phishing, so 'phishing' is true but less precise.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smishing: medium = text message.

questions.stem: An email to a payroll clerk mentions the clerk's manager by name, a real supplier the company uses, and the company's actual invoice number format, then asks for a change to the supplier's bank details. Which term BEST fits?

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: The medium is email, not SMS.

options.text: Whaling
options.rationale: Whaling targets executives; a payroll clerk isn't one.

options.text: Spear phishing
options.rationale: Correct: tailored to a specific person with real detail.

options.text: Phishing
options.rationale: True in general, but the tailoring makes a more precise term fit.

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is phishing tailored to a specific person or group, using personal detail. Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives or other high-value targets.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spear phishing is targeted and uses personal detail.

questions.stem: An email addressed to the CEO by name refers to a board meeting the CEO attended last week and asks the CEO to approve an urgent acquisition payment before the end of the day. Which term BEST fits?

options.text: Whaling
options.rationale: Correct: targeted phishing aimed at a top executive.

options.text: Spear phishing
options.rationale: Technically true, since it is targeted, but the executive target has a more precise name.

options.text: Vishing
options.rationale: The medium is email, not voice.

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: The medium is email, not text messages.

questions.explanation: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives or other high-value targets. Target seniority is what separates it from ordinary spear phishing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Whaling: target seniority is the differentiator.

questions.stem: Security footage shows a contractor walking through a badge-controlled door a step behind an employee. The employee is on a phone call and never looks back, and the contractor didn't badge. What BEST describes the breach?

options.text: Tailgating
options.rationale: Correct: the employee didn't know.

options.text: Piggybacking
options.rationale: Piggybacking needs the employee's knowledge or consent.

options.text: Social engineering
options.rationale: The umbrella category; true, but a more precise term fits.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Shoulder surfing is watching screens or keypads, not entering.

questions.explanation: Tailgating is an unauthorized person following an authorized person through a secured entry without their knowledge or consent: the victim is unknowing. Piggybacking involves consent.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tailgating: the authorized person is unaware.

questions.stem: An employee badges into the data center and holds the door for a delivery driver carrying a heavy box, saying 'go ahead, I've got it.' The driver has no badge. What BEST describes this entry?

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Shoulder surfing is visual observation, not entry.

options.text: Social engineering
options.rationale: The umbrella category; true, but not the precise term.

options.text: Tailgating
options.rationale: Tailgating happens without the employee's knowledge.

options.text: Piggybacking
options.rationale: Correct: the employee knowingly let the driver in.

questions.explanation: Piggybacking is an unauthorized person entering with an authorized person's knowledge or consent, such as when someone holds the door. Tailgating is the same entry without the authorized person knowing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Piggybacking: knowing, willing insider.

questions.stem: Which two controls MOST directly reduce the risk of someone reading a PIN or password as it is entered? (Choose two.)

options.text: Privacy filters on laptop screens
options.rationale: Correct: they block the view from the side.

options.text: Account lockout after failed attempts
options.rationale: Lockout stops guessing; an observer types the right password first time.

options.text: Encrypting traffic on the office Wi-Fi
options.rationale: Encryption protects data in transit, not a screen or keypad in view.

options.text: Shielded keypads at building entrances
options.rationale: Correct: they hide the entry from onlookers.

options.text: Passwords at least 14 characters long
options.rationale: Length resists guessing, not someone watching it typed.

questions.explanation: Shoulder surfing is observing screens or keypads to capture information. It is visual observation with no technical exploit, so the controls that work are those that block the view.
questions.discriminator_tested: Shoulder surfing is visual observation; block the view.

questions.stem: A web shop is hit by a flood from tens of thousands of botnet hosts that saturates its 1 Gbps internet link. Which two measures would MOST effectively restore service? (Choose two.)

options.text: Route traffic through a cloud DDoS scrubbing service
options.rationale: Correct: the scrubbing provider absorbs the flood and passes on clean traffic.

options.text: Block the attacking addresses on the shop's firewall
options.rationale: The link is already full before the firewall sees the traffic, and there are tens of thousands of sources.

options.text: Add more web servers behind the load balancer
options.rationale: More servers don't help when the internet link itself is saturated.

options.text: Restart the web servers to clear their sessions
options.rationale: The flood resumes the moment they come back.

options.text: Ask the ISP to filter the attack traffic upstream
options.rationale: Correct: filtering before the link removes the flood.

questions.explanation: A DDoS uses many distributed sources. Once the link itself is full, filtering has to happen upstream, at the ISP or a scrubbing service, before the traffic reaches you; a DoS from one source can be blocked locally.
questions.discriminator_tested: DDoS = many sources; filtering must happen upstream.

questions.stem: Which sequence BEST describes how a botnet is built and then used in a DDoS?

options.text: Launch the flood, compromise devices, connect them to C2
options.rationale: There is nothing to launch the flood from until devices are compromised.

options.text: Connect devices to C2, compromise them, launch the flood
options.rationale: A device only connects to the attacker's C2 after it is compromised.

options.text: Compromise devices, launch the flood, connect them to C2
options.rationale: Without C2 the devices can't be told when or what to attack.

options.text: Compromise devices, connect them to C2, launch the flood
options.rationale: Correct: devices are recruited, enrolled under control, then directed.

questions.explanation: A botnet is a network of compromised devices under attacker control. Devices are compromised first, then enrolled under command and control (C2), and only then directed at a target: the botnet is the means, not the attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: Botnet = the means: compromise, enroll under C2, then attack.

questions.stem: Malware on 40 workstations receives its instructions from a single external domain. Which action would MOST quickly cut the attacker off from these hosts while they are cleaned?

options.text: Reimage each of the 40 workstations one by one
options.rationale: Needed eventually, but slow; the hosts stay under control meanwhile.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on the access switches
options.rationale: DHCP snooping counters rogue DHCP servers, not outbound control traffic.

options.text: Reset the passwords of the 40 affected users
options.rationale: The malware doesn't need the users' passwords to take orders.

options.text: Block that domain and its IPs at the egress firewall
options.rationale: Correct: cutting the control path isolates every infected host from its orders at once.

questions.explanation: Command and control (C2) is the channel used to issue commands to compromised devices. Cutting that control path at the egress point isolates each infected host from its orders at once, buying time for cleanup.
questions.discriminator_tested: C2 is the control path; cut it to isolate compromised devices.

questions.stem: Website traffic has tripled in the last hour. Which two findings would MOST strongly suggest legitimate demand rather than an attack? (Choose two.)

options.text: Volume is three times the usual daily peak
options.rationale: Volume alone is the symptom being investigated.

options.text: Visitors browse and buy like real customers
options.rationale: Correct: real customers behave like customers.

options.text: Requests come from many different source addresses
options.rationale: Both a DDoS and a real surge come from many sources, so it decides nothing.

options.text: The surge began minutes after a marketing email went out
options.rationale: Correct: timing matches a real event that drives visitors.

options.text: Most requests hit one URL with identical headers
options.rationale: Identical, repetitive requests point toward an automated attack.

questions.explanation: A traffic spike is a symptom only; its cause may be malicious or legitimate. Timing that matches a real event and normal user behaviour point to legitimate demand; volume and many sources alone don't decide it.
questions.discriminator_tested: A traffic spike's cause can be legitimate; behaviour and timing decide it.

questions.stem: A bank's login page, payment API, and DNS provider all come under attack within the same morning. Which two observations MOST strongly indicate this is one coordinated attack rather than unrelated incidents? (Choose two.)

options.text: Forum posts show an agreed start time
options.rationale: Correct: direct evidence of planning together.

options.text: Traffic came from thousands of source addresses
options.rationale: That shows a distributed attack, not coordination between actors.

options.text: The attacks targeted services of the same bank
options.rationale: Consistent with coordination, but a popular target can attract unrelated attackers.

options.text: The different attacks began within the same minute
options.rationale: Correct: synchronized timing is the hallmark.

options.text: Each attack used a different malware family
options.rationale: Different tools say nothing about whether the actors coordinated.

questions.explanation: A coordinated attack is multiple sources or actors acting together. It overlaps with DDoS, but the emphasis is synchronization: shared timing and evidence of planning, not just many sources.
questions.discriminator_tested: Coordinated attack = synchronization between actors.

questions.stem: An internal reporting server becomes unresponsive each night around 2 a.m. No external traffic is involved. Given the output below, what is the BEST description of the root cause?
questions.exhibit:
$ crontab -l
0 2 * * *   /opt/backup/full-backup.sh
0 2 * * *   /usr/sbin/logrotate /etc/logrotate.conf

$ iostat -x 5   (sampled at 02:05)
Device   r/s     w/s     %util
sda      812.0   944.0   100.0

options.text: Resource exhaustion on the server's disk subsystem
options.rationale: True, but that is how the outage happens, not why.

options.text: An insider deliberately sabotaging the reports
options.rationale: Nothing suggests intent; the jobs are routine maintenance.

options.text: A slow DoS attack timed to avoid business hours
options.rationale: No external traffic is involved.

options.text: A scheduling mistake causing an unintentional DoS
options.rationale: Correct: two heavy jobs collide at 2 a.m.; there is no attacker.

questions.explanation: A friendly or unintentional DoS is an outage with no malicious intent, such as a misconfiguration or a runaway process. Disk exhaustion is how it happens; the overlapping schedule is why.
questions.discriminator_tested: No attacker: intent is the differentiator.

questions.stem: A colocation provider worries that someone could cut the power or cables to its customers' racks. Which control BEST addresses this threat to availability?

options.text: Redundant internet links from two providers
options.rationale: Helps if a cable is cut, but does nothing for power or physical access.

options.text: Locked cages, access logging, and redundant feeds
options.rationale: Correct: physical access control plus redundancy.

options.text: Stronger passwords on the rack PDU web pages
options.rationale: That protects against remote power-off over the network, not someone in the room.

options.text: A network IDS that alerts on unusual traffic
options.rationale: Cutting a cable creates no malicious traffic for it to see.

questions.explanation: A physical attack damages, cuts, or powers off infrastructure and hits availability with no network traffic, so network tools won't see it coming. Physical access control plus redundancy is the defence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Physical attacks need physical controls; they make no traffic.

questions.stem: A switch's firmware was deliberately corrupted and it no longer boots. Which step is needed FIRST to restore it to service?

options.text: Block the attacker's traffic at the firewall
options.rationale: Stops a flood, but this damage persists without any traffic.

options.text: Reflash the firmware or replace the switch
options.rationale: Correct: nothing else works until the device can boot.

options.text: Power-cycle the switch and wait for it to boot
options.rationale: A reboot can't repair corrupted firmware.

options.text: Restore the switch's saved configuration file
options.rationale: Needed, but only after the device can boot again.

questions.explanation: A permanent DoS corrupts device firmware so the device is unusable. A reboot won't fix it: it needs a reflash or replacement, and the configuration can only be restored after that.
questions.discriminator_tested: Permanent DoS needs reflash or replacement.

questions.stem: Your network is being used to bounce ICMP echo replies at a victim: attackers ping your broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source address. Which two measures BEST stop your network being used this way? (Choose two.)

options.text: Stop routers forwarding directed broadcasts
options.rationale: Correct: the broadcast ping never reaches your hosts.

options.text: Enable SYN cookies on the web servers
options.rationale: SYN cookies counter SYN floods, not ICMP.

options.text: Make hosts ignore broadcast pings
options.rationale: Correct: hosts that don't answer can't flood the victim.

options.text: Change the native VLAN on trunk links
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

options.text: Rate-limit ICMP traffic at the network edge
options.rationale: Reduces the volume, but still sends replies to the victim.

questions.explanation: A smurf attack sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source IP, so every host replies to the victim. Disabling directed broadcasts on routers and having hosts ignore broadcast pings removes the amplifier.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smurf needs a broadcast address that answers echo requests.
