questions.stem: A web server's connection table keeps filling with half-open TCP connections from spoofed addresses. Which measure BEST lets it keep serving real clients?

options.text: Block ICMP echo requests at the firewall
options.rationale: That addresses ICMP floods such as smurf, not TCP handshakes.

options.text: Lengthen the server's TLS keys to 4096 bits
options.rationale: Key length has nothing to do with the connection table.

options.text: Enable SYN cookies on the server
options.rationale: Correct: no table entry is held until the client completes the handshake.

options.text: Shorten the timeout for half-open connections
options.rationale: Frees entries faster but can still be outpaced by the flood.

questions.explanation: A SYN flood sends SYNs and never completes the handshake, filling the half-open connection table. SYN cookies avoid storing state until the client finishes the handshake, so spoofed SYNs can't fill the table.
questions.discriminator_tested: SYN flood fills the half-open table; SYN cookies hold no state.

questions.stem: Two attacks both use spoofed requests to third-party servers. What makes one of them amplified rather than only reflected?

options.text: A third party sends the response to the spoofed victim
options.rationale: That is reflection, which both attacks share.

options.text: The attacker's own address stays hidden from the victim
options.rationale: Also true of plain reflection.

options.text: The attack is launched from many botnet hosts at once
options.rationale: That makes an attack distributed, not amplified.

options.text: Each response is much larger than the request that caused it
options.rationale: Correct: amplification means the reply outweighs the request.

questions.explanation: In reflective and amplified attacks, spoofed requests go to third-party servers. Reflective means the third party bounces the traffic to the victim; amplified means the response is larger than the request.
questions.discriminator_tested: Amplified = response larger than request.

questions.stem: Which two measures BEST protect users from having their sessions read or altered by someone positioned between them and the server? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change the office Wi-Fi password once a month
options.rationale: Doesn't help on networks the company doesn't control.

options.text: Use a longer DHCP lease time on the network
options.rationale: Lease time has no effect on interception.

options.text: Enable account lockout after failed sign-ins
options.rationale: Lockout counters password guessing, not interception.

options.text: Tunnel remote staff traffic over a VPN
options.rationale: Correct: the tunnel can't be read or changed in transit.

options.text: Use TLS and treat certificate warnings as a stop sign
options.rationale: Correct: verified end-to-end encryption defeats an interceptor.

questions.explanation: An on-path attack (formerly MitM) places the attacker between two parties to read or alter a live session. Verified end-to-end encryption or a VPN tunnel keeps an on-path attacker from reading or silently changing traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: On-path breaks confidentiality and integrity; verified encryption defeats it.

questions.stem: Which measure BEST protects a company's resolvers from accepting forged records?

options.text: Validate responses with DNSSEC signatures
options.rationale: Correct: the resolver can verify records really came from the zone owner.

options.text: Flush the resolver cache when users complain
options.rationale: Removes poison after the damage, without preventing it.

options.text: Block outbound ICMP at the firewall
options.rationale: DNS doesn't use ICMP.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on access switches
options.rationale: That counters rogue DHCP, not forged DNS records.

questions.explanation: DNS poisoning inserts false records into a resolver or cache, so users enter the right name and reach the wrong IP. DNSSEC lets the resolver verify that records really came from the zone's owner.
questions.discriminator_tested: DNS poisoning plants false records; validate them.

questions.stem: A user's PC starts negotiating with its switch as if it were another switch, and then receives traffic from VLANs it isn't assigned to. Which method is this, and what BEST stops it?

options.text: Switch spoofing; change the trunks' native VLAN
options.rationale: Right method, wrong fix: the native VLAN matters for double tagging.

options.text: Double tagging; change the trunks' native VLAN
options.rationale: Double tagging uses stacked tags, not trunk negotiation.

options.text: Switch spoofing; disable trunk negotiation
options.rationale: Correct: an access port that can't negotiate can't become a trunk.

options.text: ARP spoofing; enable DHCP snooping on the switch
options.rationale: Nothing here involves ARP or DHCP.

questions.explanation: VLAN hopping reaches a VLAN you aren't assigned to, by switch spoofing or double tagging. Switch spoofing makes the attacker's port a trunk, so turning off negotiation stops it; double tagging exploits the native VLAN.
questions.discriminator_tested: Switch spoofing vs double tagging, and the fix for each.

questions.stem: An attacker on the guest subnet tries to redirect traffic belonging to hosts on the finance subnet, across a router, by sending forged ARP replies. Why does this fail?

options.text: ARP resolves addresses inside one local subnet
options.rationale: Correct: ARP messages don't cross the router.

options.text: Routers encrypt traffic between subnets by default
options.rationale: Routers don't encrypt traffic by default.

options.text: DHCP snooping on the finance switch blocks it
options.rationale: DHCP snooping filters DHCP offers, not ARP replies.

options.text: Router ACLs are needed to drop the forged replies
options.rationale: Routers don't forward ARP anyway; no ACL is needed.

questions.explanation: ARP spoofing sends forged ARP replies mapping the attacker's MAC to another host's IP. ARP works only on the local subnet, so the attacker must share the victim's broadcast domain.
questions.discriminator_tested: ARP spoofing is local-subnet only.

questions.stem: A laptop joins a network where an unauthorized server answers address requests faster than the real one. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Traffic routed via attacker, request sent, rogue offer accepted
options.rationale: The client has no route through the attacker until it accepts the offer.

options.text: Request sent, traffic routed via attacker, rogue offer accepted
options.rationale: The bad gateway arrives in the offer, so routing comes after acceptance.

options.text: Rogue offer accepted, request sent, traffic routed via attacker
options.rationale: A client can't accept an offer before it asks for one.

options.text: Request sent, rogue offer accepted, traffic routed via attacker
options.rationale: Correct: the client takes the first offer, then uses the rogue gateway.

questions.explanation: A rogue DHCP server is an unauthorized DHCP server that hands out a bad gateway or DNS server. The client broadcasts a request, accepts the first offer (the rogue one), then sends its traffic to the attacker's gateway. DHCP snooping counters it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rogue DHCP wins by answering first with a bad gateway.

questions.stem: A city's 900 traffic cameras join a botnet within a day of installation. The cameras were updated to the latest firmware before deployment. What is the MOST likely root cause?

options.text: The camera video feeds weren't encrypted
options.rationale: A real IoT weakness, but it exposes video rather than handing over control.

options.text: The cameras were reachable from the internet
options.rationale: An enabling condition, but exposure alone doesn't let malware in.

options.text: Factory default logins were left in place
options.rationale: Correct: with firmware current, published default credentials are the classic way in.

options.text: A rogue DHCP server gave them bad settings
options.rationale: Bad network settings wouldn't enroll devices in a botnet.

questions.explanation: IoT vulnerabilities include default credentials, unpatched firmware, and weak or no encryption, and IoT devices are a frequent source of botnet recruits. With the firmware current, unchanged default logins are the likeliest way in.
questions.discriminator_tested: IoT default credentials are a frequent source of botnet recruits.

questions.stem: Which two controls BEST detect or block an unauthorized access point plugged into an office wall jack? (Choose two.)

options.text: Training users to check the network name
options.rationale: That helps against evil twins, which target users.

options.text: WPA3 on the company's own wireless network
options.rationale: Protects the company's own Wi-Fi, not the rogue device.

options.text: Scans that flag unknown wireless APs
options.rationale: Correct: finds devices broadcasting that IT didn't install.

options.text: 802.1X authentication on wired switch ports
options.rationale: Correct: the device can't get onto the wired network without authenticating.

options.text: Changing the native VLAN on trunk ports
options.rationale: That counters double tagging.

questions.explanation: A rogue AP is an unauthorized access point plugged into the wired network, a backdoor inside it. Port authentication stops it getting network access, and wireless scanning finds it; user training addresses evil twins.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rogue AP sits inside the network; block the port, scan the air.

questions.stem: Staff often work from airports and cafes. Which control BEST protects their traffic if they connect to a fake copy of a familiar network name?

options.text: 802.1X on the office switch ports
options.rationale: That keeps rogue devices off the office LAN, not travellers safe.

options.text: Forgetting saved networks after each trip
options.rationale: Reduces automatic joining, but doesn't protect a user who joins manually.

options.text: Disabling Bluetooth on company laptops
options.rationale: Bluetooth isn't involved in joining a Wi-Fi network.

options.text: Using the company VPN on any public network
options.rationale: Correct: the twin's operator sees only encrypted tunnel traffic.

questions.explanation: An evil twin is an attacker AP imitating a legitimate SSID; it targets users. A VPN encrypts traffic end to end, so the twin's operator can't read or alter what passes through it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Evil twin targets users; protect the traffic, not the network.

questions.stem: Which two practices MOST reduce the damage an attack that encrypts company data for payment can do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disabling ICMP echo replies on the servers
options.rationale: Unrelated to encryption attacks.

options.text: Blocking common passwords at account creation
options.rationale: Good hygiene, but it doesn't limit the damage once the attack runs.

options.text: Segmentation to limit its spread
options.rationale: Correct: less of the network gets encrypted.

options.text: Cyber insurance that covers ransom payments
options.rationale: Shifts some cost, but nothing less is encrypted or lost.

options.text: Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly
options.rationale: Correct: data can be restored without paying.

questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment for the key: extortion for access. Backups the malware can't reach mean data can be restored without paying, and segmentation limits how much gets encrypted.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ransomware is extortion for access; unreachable backups remove the leverage.

questions.stem: Which control BEST prevents malware disguised as a free utility, such as a fake PDF converter, from being installed in the first place?

options.text: Allow only approved software to be installed
options.rationale: Correct: the user can't run the disguised installer.

options.text: Block ICMP at the perimeter firewall
options.rationale: Unrelated to software installation.

options.text: Patch the operating system each month
options.rationale: Patching closes flaws worms exploit; a Trojan is run by the user.

options.text: Scan downloads with up-to-date antivirus
options.rationale: Helps, but new or repackaged malware often isn't detected yet.

questions.explanation: A Trojan is malicious code disguised as legitimate software; the user must run it, and it doesn't self-replicate. Application allow-listing stops users installing disguised software in the first place.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trojan: the user must run it.

questions.stem: Self-spreading malware is exploiting a flaw in a listening service on unpatched servers. Which two actions BEST stop it spreading further? (Choose two.)

options.text: Remind users not to open unknown attachments
options.rationale: This malware spreads without any user action.

options.text: Reset the passwords of the server admins
options.rationale: It exploits a code flaw, not a password.

options.text: Block that service's port between network segments
options.rationale: Correct: cuts the path it travels on.

options.text: Patch the vulnerable service
options.rationale: Correct: removes the flaw it uses to spread.

options.text: Scan email attachments at the gateway
options.rationale: It isn't arriving by email.

questions.explanation: A worm self-replicates over networks with no user action and no host file. Removing the flaw it exploits and blocking the port it travels on stop it; user-awareness controls don't, because no user is involved.
questions.discriminator_tested: Worm needs no user action; fix the flaw and block the path.

questions.stem: Malicious code in a shared spreadsheet template copies itself into each workbook created from it. Machines whose users never open those workbooks stay clean. Which malware type BEST explains this?

options.text: Worm
options.rationale: A worm would reach machines whose users never opened anything.

options.text: Trojan
options.rationale: A Trojan doesn't copy itself into other files.

options.text: Virus
options.rationale: Correct: it rides in a host file and spreads when users open it.

options.text: Spyware
options.rationale: Nothing suggests information gathering.

questions.explanation: A virus attaches to a legitimate file or program and needs a host and user action to spread. Machines whose users never open the infected workbooks stay clean, which rules out a worm.
questions.discriminator_tested: Virus needs a host and user action.

questions.stem: Two unwanted programs are found on a laptop. What BEST distinguishes the one that is spyware from the one that is adware?

options.text: It covertly gathers user information
options.rationale: Correct: covert collection is spyware's purpose.

options.text: It is usually installed without the user's consent
options.rationale: Often true, but adware is frequently installed that way too.

options.text: It shows unwanted ads to generate revenue
options.rationale: That describes adware.

options.text: It encrypts files until a ransom is paid
options.rationale: That describes ransomware.

questions.explanation: Spyware secretly collects user activity and data; its goal is covert information gathering. Adware's focus is ads and tracking for revenue.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spyware's goal is covert information gathering.

questions.stem: Which control BEST limits the damage if malware records everything a user types, including passwords?

options.text: Multifactor authentication for remote sign-ins
options.rationale: Correct: a captured password alone no longer gets the attacker in.

options.text: Antivirus that scans for spyware
options.rationale: May detect it eventually, but doesn't limit what was already captured.

options.text: Requiring longer, more complex passwords
options.rationale: A recorded password is captured whatever its length.

options.text: Changing passwords on a 90-day cycle
options.rationale: Shortens how long a stolen password works, but it still works until then.

questions.explanation: A keylogger records keystrokes to capture credentials; it is a specific capture method, often delivered by spyware or a Trojan. Because it captures whatever is typed, a second factor the attacker can't type in is what blunts it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Keylogger captures typed input; a second factor blunts it.

questions.stem: A server is confirmed to have malware hidden at the kernel level that conceals its own files and processes. What is the BEST way to return the server to a trustworthy state?

options.text: Run a removal tool, then monitor the server closely
options.rationale: May remove it, but a tool running on the infected OS can't prove it is gone.

options.text: Patch the operating system and reboot the server
options.rationale: Patching closes the entry point but leaves the hidden malware in place.

options.text: Rebuild it from known-good media and restore clean data
options.rationale: Correct: the compromised OS can't be trusted to report on itself.

options.text: Change the administrator password on the server
options.rationale: The malware already has privileged access without the password.

questions.explanation: A rootkit hides deep in the OS, kernel, or firmware to keep privileged, stealthy access, and it is defined by concealment. Because the infected OS can't be trusted to report on itself, rebuilding from known-good media is the reliable fix.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rootkit is defined by concealment; the infected OS can't be trusted.

questions.stem: Which practice BEST prevents programs that flood staff browsers with pop-up offers from being bundled onto company PCs?

options.text: Blocking unapproved free software installs
options.rationale: Correct: the bundle never arrives.

options.text: Using an ad blocker in the web browser
options.rationale: Blocks ads on websites (the malvertising route), not installed ad software.

options.text: Running regular antivirus scans
options.rationale: Can remove it afterwards, but doesn't stop it being installed.

options.text: Changing the native VLAN on trunks
options.rationale: Unrelated to software on PCs.

questions.explanation: Adware delivers unwanted ads, often bundled with free software. Stopping unapproved installs stops the bundle arriving; an ad blocker deals with ads served on websites, the malvertising route.
questions.discriminator_tested: Adware arrives bundled with software.

questions.stem: Which control BEST protects users from malicious ads served through third-party ad networks on otherwise legitimate websites?

options.text: Ad blocking plus prompt browser patching
options.rationale: Correct: removes the delivery path and the exploit target.

options.text: Antivirus scanning of downloaded files
options.rationale: Helps if a file is downloaded, but browser exploits may not need one.

options.text: Visiting well-known, reputable websites
options.rationale: Reputable sites are exactly where these ads appear.

options.text: Blocking unapproved software installs
options.rationale: That stops bundled adware, not ads on websites.

questions.explanation: Malvertising puts malicious ads on legitimate sites, riding on ad networks; the site itself isn't compromised, so avoiding bad sites doesn't help. Blocking ads and keeping the browser patched removes the delivery path and the exploit target.
questions.discriminator_tested: Malvertising rides on ad networks; the site itself isn't compromised.

questions.stem: An online attack is working through every possible password combination for one account. Which two controls BEST defeat it? (Choose two.)

options.text: Lock the account after a few failed attempts
options.rationale: Correct: caps the number of guesses.

options.text: Block passwords found on breach lists
options.rationale: Counters dictionary attacks, which try likely passwords; an exhaustive search reaches any password.

options.text: Disable ICMP replies on the login server
options.rationale: Unrelated to password guessing.

options.text: Require long passwords or passphrases
options.rationale: Correct: makes the search space far too large.

options.text: Hash stored passwords with a fast algorithm
options.rationale: Fast hashing helps attackers who steal the hashes.

questions.explanation: Brute force tries every possible combination: exhaustive and slow. Lockouts cap the number of online guesses and length makes the search space impractically large; blocking common passwords counters dictionary attacks.
questions.discriminator_tested: Brute force is defeated by lockouts and length.

questions.stem: A honeypot that records attempted passwords logs the session below from a new attacker. Which attack BEST fits?
questions.exhibit:
10:15:02  user=admin  password=123456     result=fail
10:15:02  user=admin  password=password   result=fail
10:15:03  user=admin  password=qwerty     result=fail
10:15:03  user=admin  password=letmein    result=fail
10:15:04  user=admin  password=admin2024  result=fail

options.text: Dictionary attack
options.rationale: Correct: likely passwords from a precompiled list.

options.text: Password spraying
options.rationale: Spraying tries one common password across many accounts; this is many passwords on one account.

options.text: Brute-force attack
options.rationale: Brute force works through combinations in sequence, not popular choices.

options.text: Keylogger capture
options.rationale: A keylogger records real keystrokes; it doesn't guess.

questions.explanation: A dictionary attack tries words from a precompiled list: likely passwords such as 123456 and qwerty, not every combination. Blocking common passwords counters it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Dictionary attack guesses likely passwords, not all of them.

questions.stem: A company adds threat hunting, year-long log retention, and alerts on unusual movement between internal servers. Which threat are these controls BEST suited to uncover?

options.text: A phishing email that reaches inboxes
options.rationale: Email filtering and training target that; these controls look for what happens long after.

options.text: Users choosing weak, common passwords
options.rationale: That is addressed by password policy, not hunting.

options.text: A flood that knocks the website offline
options.rationale: A flood is loud and immediate; it doesn't need hunting.

options.text: An intruder who stays hidden for months
options.rationale: Correct: long histories and internal movement are where long-dwelling intruders show.

questions.explanation: An advanced persistent threat (APT) is a stealthy, long-term, targeted intrusion defined by persistence and dwell time. Hunting through long log histories and watching internal movement is how hidden, long-dwelling intruders are found.
questions.discriminator_tested: APT is defined by persistence and dwell time.

questions.stem: Which order of steps BEST protects a batch of new IP cameras during deployment?

options.text: Change the default login on a staging network, then deploy
options.rationale: Correct: the device is never exposed with factory credentials.

options.text: Deploy to the LAN, keeping the vendor login for support
options.rationale: Leaves a published password on every camera.

options.text: Deploy to the LAN, then block common passwords for users
options.rationale: User password policy doesn't touch the cameras' vendor login.

options.text: Deploy to the LAN, then change the default login that day
options.rationale: The login does get changed, but the device is exposed in the meantime.

questions.explanation: Changing default credentials means replacing vendor logins before deployment. Default logins are published and malware scans for them constantly, so a device exposed even briefly with factory credentials can be taken over.
questions.discriminator_tested: Change default credentials before deployment.

questions.stem: A sign-up page rejects any password found in a list of the 100,000 most common passwords. Which attack does this control MOST directly counter?

options.text: Default-login abuse
options.rationale: That is countered by changing vendor credentials.

options.text: Dictionary attack
options.rationale: Correct: it removes the passwords those lists try first.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Watching someone type works whatever the password is.

options.text: Brute-force attack
options.rationale: Exhaustive search reaches any password; lockouts and length counter it.

questions.explanation: Avoiding common passwords means blocking easily guessed passwords. It counters dictionary attacks, which try likely passwords first; brute force is defeated by lockouts and length instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Blocking common passwords counters dictionary attacks.

questions.stem: After DHCP snooping was enabled, users on VLAN 10 stop getting addresses, yet a test server on a desk port can still hand out leases. Which change BEST fixes the configuration below?
questions.exhibit:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
!
interface Gi1/0/1
 description Uplink to core (real DHCP server)
!
interface Gi1/0/12
 description User desk port
 ip dhcp snooping trust

options.text: Disable DHCP snooping so the real server can reply
options.rationale: Restores addresses but reopens the door to rogue servers.

options.text: Enable snooping on VLAN 1 as well as VLAN 10
options.rationale: Users are on VLAN 10; the trust settings are what's wrong.

options.text: Remove trust from the desk port and leave the uplink as is
options.rationale: Stops the test server, but users still get no addresses from the real one.

options.text: Trust the uplink port and remove trust from the desk port
options.rationale: Correct: offers must be accepted from the real server and refused from user ports.

questions.explanation: DHCP snooping is a switch feature that accepts DHCP offers only from trusted ports. The port toward the real server must be trusted and user ports must stay untrusted; here it is the other way round.
questions.discriminator_tested: DHCP snooping: trust the server-facing port only.

questions.stem: A network team moves the native VLAN on each trunk to VLAN 999, which carries no users. Which attack does this change MOST directly counter?

options.text: ARP spoofing on the user VLAN
options.rationale: ARP spoofing works within one VLAN whatever the native VLAN is.

options.text: VLAN hopping by double tagging
options.rationale: Correct: the attacker's outer tag can no longer match the native VLAN.

options.text: VLAN hopping of any kind
options.rationale: True for one method only; switch spoofing needs negotiation disabled.

options.text: VLAN hopping by switch spoofing
options.rationale: Switch spoofing is stopped by disabling trunk negotiation.

questions.explanation: Changing the native VLAN moves it off the default, which counters double-tagging VLAN hopping: the attacker's outer tag no longer matches the native VLAN. Switch spoofing is stopped by disabling trunk negotiation.
questions.discriminator_tested: Changing the native VLAN counters double tagging.

questions.stem: A server was compromised through a flaw the vendor had fixed eight months earlier. The server had antivirus, a firewall, and strong passwords. What is the BEST statement of the root cause?

options.text: The firewall allowed traffic to the vulnerable service
options.rationale: A contributing factor, but the service had to be reachable to do its job.

options.text: The vendor's fix wasn't applied to the server
options.rationale: Correct: the flaw was known and fixable.

options.text: The server's firmware was out of date
options.rationale: The flaw was in software the vendor fixed, not in firmware.

options.text: The antivirus definitions were too old
options.rationale: Antivirus isn't designed to close software flaws.

questions.explanation: Patching and updating fixes known software vulnerabilities. A fix available for eight months means the flaw was known; failing to apply it is the root cause, whatever other controls were in place.
questions.discriminator_tested: Patching fixes known software vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: Which two of these flaws are fixed by upgrading firmware rather than by patching software? (Choose two.)

options.text: A bug in the server's operating system
options.rationale: Fixed by an OS patch.

options.text: A flaw in a switch's boot code
options.rationale: Correct: boot code is embedded device-level code.

options.text: A weak password on a router admin page
options.rationale: A configuration problem, not a code flaw.

options.text: A flaw in a web browser
options.rationale: An application, fixed by a software update.

options.text: A bug in a hard drive controller's code
options.rationale: Correct: controller code lives on the device.

questions.explanation: Upgrading firmware updates device-level code embedded in hardware, such as boot code or a drive controller. OS and application flaws are fixed by patching software.
questions.discriminator_tested: Firmware is device-level code; OS and apps are patched.

questions.stem: A company relies on one perimeter firewall for protection. Inside, the servers share one flat network, users are local admins, and there is no endpoint protection. Which principle is it MOST clearly failing to apply?

options.text: Network segmentation
options.rationale: Also missing, but it too is one layer within the bigger principle.

options.text: Defense in depth
options.rationale: Correct: one control is relied on for everything.

options.text: Least privilege
options.rationale: Also missing, but it is one of the absent layers, not the overall principle.

options.text: Separation of duties
options.rationale: Splitting tasks between people isn't what's described.

questions.explanation: Defense in depth uses layered, overlapping controls so that no single control is relied on. Here one firewall is the only layer; segmentation and least privilege are missing layers within that principle.
questions.discriminator_tested: Defense in depth: no single control is relied on.

questions.stem: Which control BEST reduces the success of attacks that manipulate employees into giving away access?

options.text: Multifactor authentication on user accounts
options.rationale: Limits what a stolen password achieves, but doesn't stop the manipulation.

options.text: Stronger encryption on the office Wi-Fi
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't stop someone being talked into helping.

options.text: Patching operating systems each month
options.rationale: Patching fixes system flaws, not human ones.

options.text: Realistic awareness training
options.rationale: Correct: it targets the people being manipulated.

questions.explanation: Social engineering manipulates people rather than systems, so the most direct control trains people to recognise and report it. MFA limits what a stolen password achieves but doesn't stop the manipulation itself.
questions.discriminator_tested: Social engineering targets people; train people.

questions.stem: Which two controls MOST directly limit the harm that staff who already have legitimate access can do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Log and review privileged user activity
options.rationale: Valuable for detection and deterrence, but it records harm rather than limiting it.

options.text: Prompt removal of leavers' access
options.rationale: Correct: closes access that is no longer needed.

options.text: A stronger perimeter firewall
options.rationale: Insiders are already inside the perimeter.

options.text: Blocking common passwords
options.rationale: Insiders use their own valid credentials.

options.text: Give each role only the access it needs
options.rationale: Correct: least privilege limits what any one person can damage.

questions.explanation: Insider threats are harm from someone with legitimate access, malicious or accidental; they're already inside the perimeter. Least privilege limits what each person can damage and prompt deprovisioning closes unneeded access; monitoring detects misuse rather than limiting it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Insiders are already inside the perimeter.

questions.stem: An employee clicked a link in a fake 'password expiry' email and entered their password on the page it opened. What should happen FIRST?

options.text: Block the sender and the link at the email gateway
options.rationale: Needed to protect others, but the exposed credential comes first.

options.text: Reimage the employee's laptop to remove malware
options.rationale: Nothing suggests malware; a password was typed into a fake page.

options.text: Reset the employee's password and end active sessions
options.rationale: Correct: the password is compromised and may already be in use.

options.text: Enroll the employee in awareness training
options.rationale: Useful afterwards, but it doesn't contain the exposure.

questions.explanation: Phishing uses fraudulent messages to steal data or credentials. Once a password has been entered on a fake page it is compromised, so resetting it and ending sessions comes first; blocking and training follow.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phishing steals credentials; contain the exposed credential first.

questions.stem: Callers claiming to be from IT keep phoning staff and asking them for their one-time sign-in codes. Which control BEST counters this?

options.text: Longer passwords for staff accounts
options.rationale: The callers want the codes, and length doesn't stop a person reading one out.

options.text: An email filter that blocks spoofed senders
options.rationale: The attack arrives by phone, not email.

options.text: Multifactor authentication on staff accounts
options.rationale: Already in place; the codes it produces are what the callers are stealing.

options.text: A rule to hang up and ring back on a known number
options.rationale: Correct: a call-back to a known number defeats an impersonator.

questions.explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice or phone. Because the medium is a phone call, the defence is a process people follow on calls: verify the caller through a known number before sharing anything.
questions.discriminator_tested: Vishing: medium = voice; verify the caller.

questions.stem: Which two of these are smishing? (Choose two.)

options.text: A text saying a parcel is held, with a short link
options.rationale: Correct: phishing by text message.

options.text: A bank 'security' SMS asking for a code
options.rationale: Correct: phishing by SMS.

options.text: A stranger watching you enter your phone PIN
options.rationale: That is shoulder surfing.

options.text: A phone call from 'IT' asking for your password
options.rationale: Voice is vishing.

options.text: An email from 'HR' with a fake benefits form link
options.rationale: Email is ordinary phishing.

questions.explanation: Smishing is phishing by SMS or text message: the medium is the text. Calls are vishing, and emails are ordinary phishing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smishing: medium = text message.

questions.stem: An attacker researches a finance team on social media and sends each member an email that refers to their real projects and colleagues. Which control BEST reduces this risk?

options.text: Require complex passwords for finance staff
options.rationale: Doesn't stop staff being persuaded to act on a request.

options.text: Verify requests through a second channel
options.rationale: Correct: independent verification works however convincing the email is.

options.text: Block attachments with macros at the gateway
options.rationale: Many tailored emails carry no attachment at all.

options.text: Filter emails from newly registered look-alike domains
options.rationale: Helps, but a tailored email can come from a compromised real account.

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is phishing tailored to a specific person or group, using personal detail so it looks credible. Independent verification through a known channel defeats it, however convincing the email is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spear phishing is targeted; verify independently.

questions.stem: An attacker phones the CFO's assistant pretending to be the CEO, then emails the CFO a personalised request to wire funds before a deadline. Which part of this campaign is whaling?

options.text: The tailored email to the CFO
options.rationale: Correct: targeted phishing aimed at a senior executive.

options.text: The phone call to the assistant
options.rationale: That is vishing aimed at a non-executive.

options.text: The research into the executives
options.rationale: Reconnaissance supports the attack but isn't phishing itself.

options.text: The whole campaign taken as one
options.rationale: The campaign mixes techniques; only one part targets an executive by email.

questions.explanation: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives or other high-value targets; target seniority is the differentiator. The call to the assistant is vishing aimed at a non-executive.
questions.discriminator_tested: Whaling: target seniority is the differentiator.

questions.stem: Which control BEST stops unauthorized people slipping through a secure door behind staff who don't notice them?

options.text: A one-person-per-badge turnstile
options.rationale: Correct: enforces one entry per badge whether staff notice or not.

options.text: Training staff not to hold doors open
options.rationale: Helps with piggybacking, but these staff never notice anyone.

options.text: Privacy screens on the reception PCs
options.rationale: Privacy screens stop shoulder surfing.

options.text: Security cameras recording the entrance
options.rationale: Records the breach but doesn't stop it.

questions.explanation: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured entry without their knowledge or consent. Because the employee doesn't notice, training can't help; a mantrap or one-person turnstile physically enforces one entry per badge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tailgating: unknowing victim; enforce one entry per badge.

questions.stem: Staff often hold the server-room door open for colleagues and visitors who say they forgot their badges. Which control BEST addresses this behaviour?

options.text: Shielded keypads at the server-room door
options.rationale: Shielded keypads stop shoulder surfing.

options.text: Cameras that record who enters the room
options.rationale: Creates a record but doesn't change what staff do.

options.text: Policy: each person badges in
options.rationale: Correct: staff are choosing to let people in, so change the behaviour.

options.text: Stronger encryption on the badge cards
options.rationale: The people let in aren't using badges at all.

questions.explanation: Piggybacking is entry with an authorized person's knowledge or consent, such as holding the door. Because the employee chooses to let someone in, the fix is policy and training that make each person badge in; a turnstile also helps.
questions.discriminator_tested: Piggybacking: knowing, willing insider.

questions.stem: A user's banking password is used fraudulently. The user never typed it on a shared device, no malware is found, and the password wasn't reused, but the user often signs in on a laptop on a crowded commuter train. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: A keylogger recorded the keystrokes
options.rationale: No malware was found on the laptop.

options.text: A dictionary attack guessed the password
options.rationale: A unique, unreused password is unlikely to be on a guess list.

options.text: Someone watched the password being typed
options.rationale: Correct: a crowded train is ideal for observation.

options.text: A smishing text tricked the user into sharing it
options.rationale: The user would remember sending it in reply to a text.

questions.explanation: Shoulder surfing is observing screens or keypads to capture information. It is visual observation with no technical exploit, which fits a clean laptop used in a crowded place.
questions.discriminator_tested: Shoulder surfing is visual observation; no technical exploit.

questions.stem: An attacker has stolen a password-hash file and is hashing each entry of a 14-million-word leaked-password list to find matches. Which control, in place before the theft, would MOST reduce how many accounts this cracks?

options.text: Rejecting passwords found on breach lists
options.rationale: Correct: if no account uses a listed password, the list finds nothing.

options.text: Requiring passwords of at least 8 characters
options.rationale: Many leaked passwords, such as 'Summer2024!', already meet length rules.

options.text: Locking accounts after five failed logins
options.rationale: The guessing happens offline against the stolen file; no login is ever attempted.

options.text: Forcing a password change each quarter
options.rationale: Changes on a schedule don't stop a listed password being cracked today.

questions.explanation: A dictionary attack tries words from a precompiled list: it guesses likely passwords, not all of them. Offline, lockouts never trigger; what defeats it is making sure no account uses a password that appears on such lists.
questions.discriminator_tested: Dictionary attack guesses likely passwords; block listed passwords.

questions.stem: A smurf attack and a DNS amplification attack both send spoofed requests that make third parties flood a victim. What BEST distinguishes the smurf attack?

options.text: It uses the victim's spoofed source address
options.rationale: True, but both attacks do this, so it doesn't distinguish them.

options.text: It relies on open resolvers returning large answers
options.rationale: That describes DNS amplification.

options.text: It leaves TCP handshakes unfinished on the victim
options.rationale: That describes a SYN flood.

options.text: It sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address
options.rationale: Correct: every host on the segment replies to the spoofed victim.

questions.explanation: A smurf attack sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source IP, so the victim is flooded by replies from many hosts. Both it and DNS amplification are spoofed reflection attacks; the broadcast echo is what makes it a smurf.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smurf: ICMP echo to a broadcast address.
